title: 22. Interview: Functional Requirements vs Non-Functional Requirements
summary: Interview Q&A for Functional Requirements vs Non-Functional Requirements — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Functional Requirements vs Non-Functional Requirements interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. In one sentence each, define functional and non-functional requirements, then give an example of each for a URL shortener.
**Answer:** A functional requirement states a behavior the system must exhibit; a non-functional requirement states a quality the system must have while exhibiting that behavior. For a URL shortener, an FR is: "given a long URL, the system returns a unique 7-character short code and, on subsequent request of that code, redirects to the original long URL." An NFR is: "the redirect endpoint must respond in under 30 ms at p99 and remain available 99.99% of the time." The FR is testable by an assertion on the response; the NFR is testable by a load and uptime measurement over a month. The FR could be satisfied by a single Python process on a laptop; the NFR forces a load balancer, a cache, and at least two replicas. Strip away the NFR and the architecture collapses to its simplest form.

**Visual:**
```
FR:  POST /shorten {url} -> {code} ;  GET /:code   -> 302 redirect
NFR: p99 < 30ms ; uptime >= 99.99% ; scale 10K QPS
```

### Q2. What is the USARI checklist and why is it useful in interviews?
**Answer:** USARI stands for Usability, Availability, Scalability, Reliability, Integrity — five categories of NFRs that, taken together, cover most of what an architecture must satisfy. Usability covers accessibility, internationalization, and UX responsiveness. Availability covers uptime, failover, and SLA. Scalability covers throughput, concurrency, and growth. Reliability covers durability, consistency, idempotency, and MTBF. Integrity covers security, audit, and compliance. The checklist is useful in interviews because it gives the candidate a script to elicit NFRs systematically rather than waiting for the interviewer to volunteer them. After stating the FRs, the candidate says: "Now let me check the NFRs across USARI — what's the availability target, expected scale, latency budget, consistency requirement, and compliance posture?" This single sentence often reshapes the entire design and signals seniority. The exact acronym is less important than the habit.

**Visual:**
```
U  Usability      (accessibility, i18n, UX latency)
S  Scalability    (QPS, concurrency, growth)
A  Availability   (uptime, failover, SLA)
R  Reliability    (durability, consistency, idempotency)
I  Integrity      (security, audit, compliance)
```

### Q3. Why are NFRs more expensive to retrofit late than FRs?
**Answer:** An FR is usually additive — a new endpoint, a new field, a new screen. It can be shipped in a sprint and rolls back cleanly. An NFR is structural — it constrains every component. Retrofitting 99.99% availability onto a system designed for 99% means moving from single-region to multi-region active-active, which touches deployment, data replication, DNS failover, and operational runbooks — a multi-quarter effort with no user-visible feature shipped. Retrofitting sub-50 ms latency onto a chatty synchronous service means re-architecting the call graph, introducing caches, and probably moving to async messaging. Retrofitting strong consistency onto an eventually consistent store means rewriting the data layer. The cost is non-linear: an NFR baked in at design time costs roughly 1x; the same NFR retrofitted at year three costs 5–10x because of migration, dual-running, and the risk of breaking existing users. That is why extracting NFRs up front is the highest-leverage minute in any design session.

**Visual:**
```
Cost to satisfy an NFR
   ^
   |                                  /
   |                                /
   |                              /
   |                          /
   |                    /
   |              /
   |        /  (late retrofit: 5-10x)
   +------------------------------------> time
     design    launch    year 3
```

### Q4. How do you make an NFR testable? Give an example for "the system should be highly available."
**Answer:** "Highly available" is not testable — it is a wish. To make it testable, attach three things: a number, a measurement window, and a measurement method. The rewritten NFR is: "the API endpoints in scope will be available ≥ 99.95% per calendar month, measured as successful HTTP responses (status < 500) divided by total requests, aggregated across regions, with planned maintenance windows of < 4 hours per quarter excluded." Now it is testable: an external probe (e.g., CloudWatch Synthetics or Pingdom) hits a health-check endpoint every minute, divides successes by total, and alerts if the monthly ratio drops below 99.95%. The same pattern applies to every NFR: latency becomes "p99 < 200 ms for the top 5 endpoints, measured at the load balancer over a 5-minute window"; scalability becomes "sustained 10K QPS with CPU < 70% on a 6-node fleet during a 30-minute load test." Without numbers and windows, NFRs degrade into aspirational comments in a README that nobody reads.

**Visual:**
```
wish:        "highly available"
              |
              v
number:      99.95%
              |
              v
window:      per calendar month
              |
              v
method:      synthetic probe / (success / total), excludes planned maint
              |
              v
alert:       PagerDuty if ratio < 99.95% mid-month
```

### Q5. Give an example of a conflict between two NFRs and how you resolve it.
**Answer:** A classic conflict is **strong consistency** vs **low latency** in a globally distributed system. CAP theorem tells us that during a network partition we must choose; even without a partition, PACELC tells us we pay a latency cost for consistency on every write. If the NFRs say "all regions see the same value within 100 ms" and "p99 write latency < 50 ms," those two are in tension globally — a synchronous cross-region quorum adds 50–150 ms of network round-trip. Resolution options: (1) weaken one NFR — accept eventual consistency with a 1-second convergence window, which is fine for a profile photo; (2) scope the NFR — require strong consistency only within a region, and eventual consistency across regions (the typical social-feed pattern); (3) redesign — use a single global primary for the conflicting data class, accepting that writes from far-away regions pay higher latency. The resolution is always product-driven: ask "what does the user actually need?" and downgrade the NFR that the user will not notice.

**Visual:**
```
Strong consistency  <--conflict-->  Low p99 latency
        |                                  |
        v                                  v
single global primary               regional primaries + async repl
(p99 write high far from primary)   (brief divergence accepted)
```

### Q6. What NFRs does Netflix publicly commit to for playback, and how do they shape the architecture?
**Answer:** Netflix commits to roughly **99.99% availability** (about 52 minutes of downtime per year) and **<100 ms playback startup latency** at p95 globally. These two NFRs shape the architecture in concrete ways. The availability target forces multi-region active-active deployment on AWS — each region can serve all subscribers if the other fails, and traffic shifts via DNS in minutes. The latency target forces a CDN-first design: Open Connect appliances are physically placed inside ISP networks so the first video segment comes from a box within milliseconds of the user, not from a regional origin. The latency target also drives aggressive pre-fetching — when a user hovers over a title, the client pre-fetches the manifest and the first segments. The availability target drives chaos engineering (the Simian Army) — Netflix intentionally kills instances and entire zones in production to verify the NFR holds under failure. None of these decisions follow from the FR "user can play a movie"; they all follow from the two NFRs.

**Visual:**
```
NFR: avail 99.99%  --> multi-region active-active + chaos eng (Simian Army)
NFR: latency <100ms--> Open Connect CDN at ISP + hover prefetch
FR:  play movie    --> (alone, would be a single origin server)
```

### Q7. How do you elicit NFRs from a stakeholder who says "just make it fast and reliable"?
**Answer:** Translate vague adjectives into numbers via comparison questions. For "fast," ask: "Faster than what? Faster than our competitor? What is the user doing — if they are tapping a button on mobile, 200 ms feels instant; if they are submitting a batch report, 30 seconds may be fine. What is the budget we are willing to pay for — a CDN cuts 100 ms but costs $X/month." For "reliable," ask: "Reliable like a consumer website (99.9% — 8.7 h downtime/year) or like an emergency-services system (99.999% — 5 min/year)? What is the cost of one hour of downtime in revenue and trust?" Force the stakeholder to pick a number by anchoring: "Most teams in our situation pick 99.95%; does that feel right or too lax?" Then write the number down and read it back. The job is not to extract perfect numbers — it is to replace adjectives with measurable targets the team can design and test against. A wrong number you can renegotiate; a vague adjective you cannot.

**Visual:**
```
Stakeholder: "make it fast and reliable"
            |
            v  (anchor with comparison)
Q: faster than competitor X?  reliable like 911 or like a blog?
            |
            v  (force a number)
99.95% / month, p99 < 200ms  <-- write it down, read it back
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your team is building an internal employee directory. The PM says "make it as available as our customer-facing site, 99.99%." Push back appropriately.
**Answer:** I would push back by quantifying the cost of the NFR. A 99.99% availability target allows about 52 minutes of downtime per year — which forces multi-region active-active deployment, automated failover, and on-call rotations with paged response in under 15 minutes, 24×7. For a customer-facing e-commerce site, that cost is justified by revenue. For an internal employee directory used during business hours, 99.9% (8.7 hours/year, almost all of which can be scheduled overnight) is more than enough — and the engineering and on-call cost is perhaps 1/5th. I would ask the PM: "What happens if the directory is down for 2 hours during a Tuesday afternoon?" If the answer is "people complain but use Slack DMs to find each other," the NFR should be 99.9%, not 99.99%. The principle: NFRs should be proportional to the cost of not meeting them. Over-committing burns engineering budget that should go to features with actual user value.

**Visual:**
```
99.99% (52 min/yr)  -> multi-region active-active, 24x7 on-call  (cost: $$$$)
99.9%  (8.7 h/yr)   -> single region + replicas, business-hours on-call  (cost: $$)
99%   (3.65 d/yr)   -> single AZ, best-effort  (cost: $)

Employee directory during business hours? -> 99.9% is the right target.
```

### Q2. You are designing a payments service. The CFO demands 99.999% availability because "money is on the line." Walk through your response.
**Answer:** I would first acknowledge that the underlying concern is legitimate — payment unavailability directly blocks revenue and damages trust. But I would challenge the number itself: 99.999% is 5.26 minutes of downtime per year, which exceeds what even major payment networks publicly commit to (Visa and Mastercard typically target 99.99% measured over a year). The cost of 99.999% is enormous — multi-region active-active with synchronous cross-region replication, redundant vendor paths, 24×7 senior on-call, and rigorous change-management gates that slow feature velocity. More importantly, I would argue that for payments the dominant NFR is not raw availability but **integrity**: never double-charge, never lose a transaction, never show an incorrect balance. A 30-minute outage with zero data loss is far better than a 5-minute outage that double-charged 10,000 customers. I would propose 99.99% availability paired with strong idempotency, durable event-sourced state, and reconciliation jobs. The right NFR for payments is "no financial data loss, ever" — availability is a means to that end, not the end itself.

**Visual:**
```
CFO asks: 99.999% availability
Engineer reframes:
   Primary NFR = INTEGRITY (no double-charge, no lost txns, durable audit)
   Secondary   = AVAILABILITY 99.99% (still strong, but bounded cost)
   Outage plan = degraded modes: queue payments, retry, reconcile
```

### Q3. A startup wants to launch a TikTok-clone and asks for "sub-100ms video start." Your back-of-the-envelope says global origin serving is impossible. What do you do?
**Answer:** I would treat the NFR as the constraint that drives the architecture, not as a number to negotiate down. The math: 100 ms is roughly the budget for one cross-region network round trip plus one disk read; serving video from a single origin cannot meet it for users far from that origin. The architecture must be CDN-first: video segments are pre-distributed to CDN edges close to users, and the manifest is generated near the user so the first segment request hits a cache within a few milliseconds. I would push the NFR back on the PM in two specific ways. First, "sub-100 ms" should be qualified — at what percentile, in which regions, on what network? A p95 in the US on fiber is achievable; a p99 in rural India on 3G is not, and pretending otherwise wastes engineering effort. Second, I would separate "time to first byte" from "time to first frame" — the latter includes client decode, which the server cannot control. The negotiated NFR becomes "TTFB < 100 ms at p95 in the top 10 markets," which is measurable, fair, and drives the right architecture.

**Visual:**
```
Original NFR:    "sub-100ms video start"  (ambiguous, unmeasurable)
Renegotiated:    "TTFB < 100ms at p95 in top-10 markets"
                       |
                       v
Architecture:    CDN-first (segments at edge) + regional manifest generation
```

### Q4. You inherit a system with 200 un-documented NFRs scattered across Jira tickets. How do you recover?
**Answer:** I would run a three-step recovery. First, **mine** the existing artifacts: grep the codebase for `SLA`, `latency`, `p99`, `availability`; read past incident postmortems (they reveal the NFRs the system actually cares about); read customer contracts for SLA clauses. Cluster the findings into USARI categories. Second, **rationalize**: for each candidate NFR, ask whether it is still relevant — many will be stale (a 5-year-old retention rule for a feature that was deprecated). For each survivor, attach a number, a window, and a measurement method; if you cannot, delete it. Third, **publish**: consolidate into a single living document (an "SLO catalog") that lists each NFR, its owner, its test, and its current compliance. Host it next to the architecture diagram, not in a Confluence page nobody opens. The deliverable is not "all 200 NFRs documented" — it is "the 20 NFRs that actually constrain the architecture, each testable, each owned." The other 180 were noise; recovering means deleting confidently, not cataloging exhaustively.

**Visual:**
```
200 scattered tickets  -->  MINE (grep + postmortems + contracts)
                       -->  RATIONALIZE (delete stale; attach numbers)
                       -->  PUBLISH (SLO catalog: owner + test + status)
                       -->  ~20 NFRs that actually shape architecture
```

### Q5. Your service is sold to two customer segments: enterprises who want 99.99% availability and SMBs who want cheap. One architecture cannot serve both NFRs cheaply. What do you do?
**Answer:** I would treat the two NFR profiles as a product-segmentation signal that should be reflected in the architecture, not papered over. The cleanest pattern is a tiered deployment: an enterprise tier running multi-region active-active with synchronous replication, dedicated capacity, and 24×7 on-call; and an SMB tier running single-region best-effort with shared capacity and business-hours support. Both tiers run the same code; they differ in deployment topology and operational investment. This is how AWS itself structures offerings (Single-AZ vs Multi-AZ RDS, standard vs enterprise support). The pricing reflects the NFR differential — enterprise pays 5–10x because the underlying cost is 5–10x. The alternative — one architecture sized for the strictest NFR and priced for everyone — either prices SMBs out or subsidizes them at a loss. The system-design lesson: when two customer segments demand materially different NFR profiles, the architecture itself should bifurcate; trying to satisfy both with one design produces a system that is over-built for one and over-priced for the other.

**Visual:**
```
                   shared codebase
                          |
              +-----------+-----------+
              v                       v
   Enterprise tier               SMB tier
   multi-region A-A              single-region best-effort
   99.99% SLA                    99.5% SLA
   $$$$                          $
   (dedicated capacity)          (shared capacity)
```

### Q6. A regulation now requires "all user data must be deletable within 30 days of request" (GDPR-style). Translate this into NFRs that drive architecture.
**Answer:** "Deletable within 30 days" decomposes into several concrete NFRs. First, **completeness**: every store that holds personal data — primary DB, read replicas, backups, search index, analytics warehouse, ML training datasets, caches, logs — must support deletion, or the regulation is not met. This forces a data-inventory NFR: "the system maintains a registry of every store containing user PII, with a deletion procedure per store." Second, **timeliness**: 30 days is the outer bound, but backups typically roll on a 7–35 day cycle, so the architecture must support either point-in-time logical deletion on restore or a backup window short enough to meet 30 days. Third, **auditability**: deletion must be provable on request — "we deleted user X on date Y from stores A, B, C." This forces an immutable audit log of deletion events. Fourth, **integrity**: deletion must not corrupt referential data — if user X authored comments, those comments must either be hard-deleted, anonymized, or retained with author stripped. The original one-line regulation thus becomes four NFRs that drive a data lineage map, a tombstone pattern, and a deletion pipeline.

**Visual:**
```
Regulation: "deletable within 30 days"
   |
   +--> NFR1 Completeness: registry of every PII store
   +--> NFR2 Timeliness: backup window <= 30d OR logical delete-on-restore
   +--> NFR3 Auditability: immutable deletion audit log
   +--> NFR4 Integrity: tombstone or anonymize referential data
   |
   v
Architecture: data lineage map + tombstone pattern + deletion pipeline
```

### Q7. Your team's API latency spiked 3x after a viral TikTok. The FRs are all still met (responses are correct), but the NFR is broken. How do you frame the incident?
**Answer:** I would frame it explicitly as an NFR violation, not a bug. The system is functionally correct — every response is right — but it is failing its latency NFR ("p99 < 200 ms"), which is a real production failure even though no test in the FR suite caught it. This framing matters because it dictates the response: a bug hunt would waste time looking for logic errors; an NFR violation calls for capacity analysis (did traffic exceed the designed QPS?), saturation analysis (which tier hit CPU/conn-pool limits?), and a redesign if the load is the new normal. I would update the postmortem to call out that the FR test suite passed but the NFR test suite (load tests, latency probes) either did not exist or did not run at scale — and the action item is to add continuous load testing that simulates viral spikes. The deeper lesson for the team: an incident with correct responses can still be a severe outage if a published NFR is broken; NFRs are first-class citizens, not nice-to-haves.

**Visual:**
```
Incident classification:
   FR tests:    PASS  (every response correct)
   NFR (p99):   FAIL  (200ms budget -> 600ms observed)
        |
        v
   Response = capacity & saturation analysis, NOT bug hunt
   Action  = add continuous load test that simulates viral spikes
```
